title: Nyame, Asase Yaa and the Making of the World
source_ref: Akan oral tradition; variants recorded in R. S. Rattray, Ashanti (1923), and J. B. Danquah, The Akan Doctrine of God (1944)
paragraphs: Akan accounts of the beginning do not agree, and no single version is authoritative. In most, Nyame, whose name is linked to the sky, is the supreme being, and Asase Yaa is the earth. Some tellers say Nyame made the world; others say the world was already there and Nyame set it in order. Both powers are older than the first people.

When Nyame made the first man and woman, one account says he lowered them from the sky on a golden chain. Another says they came up through a hole in the ground. He gave them breath, a body and a destiny, and he set them on the earth that Asase Yaa holds. The first people learned farming, fire and law from what they were given.

The world was ordered by relationship. Nyame stayed in the sky, and the abosom, the lesser powers of rivers, rocks and trees, carried prayers between the sky and the earth. Asase Yaa received the dead and gave the living their food. Each person carried a spirit, the ancestors remained part of the household, and Thursday was the earth's day.

The accounts are many. In one widely told story, Nyame withdrew from the sky because a woman pounding fufu kept striking him with her pestle, and that is why the sky is now far away. Rattray, Danquah and later Akan writers record different versions, and Christian and traditional understandings now sit side by side. This retelling is a synthesis, not a fixed text.
notes: There is no single Akan creation text. Rattray, Danquah and later Akan writers record different emphases: whether Nyame made the world or ordered an existing one, whether the first people came down a golden chain or up through the ground, and whether Asase Yaa is Nyame's wife, his creation or a separate power. The sky's withdrawal is a separate etiological story. This account is a synthesis of recorded variants.

title: Ananse and the Sky God's Stories
source_ref: Akan folktale cycle (anansesem); versions in R. S. Rattray, Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales (1930) and Ghanaian collections such as Peggy Appiah's Ananse the Spider
paragraphs: In the beginning people had no stories. All the stories in the world belonged to Nyame, who kept them in the sky, and Ananse the spider decided to buy them. He climbed to Nyame's court and asked the price. Nyame named three creatures: Onini the python, the swarm of hornets called Mmoboro, and Osebo the leopard. Ananse, who was small and greedy and very sure of himself, agreed.

For the python, Ananse cut a long pole and carried it to the river. He argued that Onini could not possibly be as long as the pole, and the python, insulted, stretched himself along it to prove his size. Ananse tied him to the pole with vine before he could coil. He carried the python up to Nyame and asked for the first part of his payment.

For the hornets, Ananse poured water over their tree and called out that the rain had come. He offered them a calabash to shelter in, and when the swarm had crawled inside he sealed it. For the leopard, he dug a pit on the path Osebo used and covered it with leaves. The leopard fell in, and Ananse delivered him too, though not without a struggle.

Nyame kept his word. He gave Ananse the stories and named them after him: anansesem, spider stories. But Ananse did not become wise or generous. In most tellings he is still hungry, still boasting, and still laughed at by the people who repeat his tales. The stories he won are still told, and the version Rattray recorded adds a fairy and Ananse's own mother to the price.

title: Ananse and the Pot of Wisdom
source_ref: Akan folktale, widely told in Ghana and the Caribbean; recorded variants in Rattray and later collections
paragraphs: Ananse decided to gather all the wisdom in the world. He travelled from village to village, listening at doors and in markets, and every clever thing he heard he put into a clay pot. When the pot was full, he looked at it and thought: this is mine. If I keep it at the top of the tallest tree, no one else can ever be wise.

He tied the pot to his chest with a rope and began to climb. The pot was heavy. It slipped against the bark, and his hands could not reach around it to grip the trunk. He tried again from the other side, then from a lower branch, and each time the pot swung and dragged him down. He would not leave it on the ground.

His small son Ntikuma watched from below. 'Father,' he said, 'why not tie the pot on your back, so your arms are free?' Ananse stopped. He had collected every kind of wisdom except the wisdom to listen to a child. He was so angry that he shouted, and the pot slipped from his chest.

It broke on the ground, and the wisdom spilled out and scattered. The wind took some, the rain washed some into the rivers, and people walking past picked up pieces. That is why no one person is wise in everything, and why good advice may come from a child. Some tellers use a calabash instead of a pot, and some name a different son, but the ending is the same.
notes: The tale exists in several forms: the container may be a pot or a calabash, the child may be named Ntikuma or left unnamed, and some tellers have Ananse blame the boy rather than himself. The moral is drawn variously as a comment on hoarding, on the limits of cleverness, or on listening to the young.

title: The Golden Stool
source_ref: Asante historical tradition, as recorded from the early twentieth century; modern histories by Ivor Wilks (1975) and T. C. McCaskie (1995)
paragraphs: In the late seventeenth century the Akan states around Kumasi were separate and often at war. Osei Tutu was their war leader; Okomfo Anokye was his priest. Anokye told the assembled chiefs that the nation needed a soul. He called on Nyame, and a stool covered in gold came down from the sky and landed on Osei Tutu's lap. That day was a Friday, so the stool was named Sika Dwa Kofi.

The stool was not a throne. No one sits on it, not even the king. It is understood as the sunsum, the spirit, of the whole Asante nation, and the Asantehene rules in its name rather than from it. The chiefs accepted it, and the Asante union took shape with Kumasi at its centre. The stool became the thing the nation defended first.

Because it is sacred, the stool is not displayed like a museum piece. It has its own custodians and appears in public only on rare occasions, and the details of its care are not for outsiders. When the nation was threatened, people hid it rather than surrender it. To sit on it, or even to touch it without right, is understood as an attack on the nation itself.

The descent from the sky is tradition, told for generations before it was written down; it is not a contemporary record, and the founding of the union is usually dated to about 1700. The kingdom it founded was real and powerful. In 1896 Britain exiled the Asantehene, and in 1900 a governor demanded the stool; Yaa Asantewaa led the war that followed. It remains sacred today.
notes: Okomfo Anokye is a historical figure of the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, but the account of the stool's descent is traditional and was written down much later. The founding date is usually given as about 1700, though the battle of Feyiase is dated 1701 and the number of founding states varies. This retelling deliberately omits ritual detail that is not for outsiders.

title: The First Akua'ba
source_ref: Akan oral tradition; ethnographic and museum accounts of akua'ba figures, including Herbert M. Cole and Doran H. Ross, The Arts of Ghana (1977)
paragraphs: Akua had no child, and she wanted one badly. She went for advice, and she was told that her hope had to be carried, not merely felt: she should have a small figure carved from wood, wrap it in cloth, and care for it as she would care for a baby. Some say a priest gave this advice; others say an old woman did. Akua did as she was told.

She carried the figure on her back, tied with cloth the way a mother carries a child. She bathed it, fed it, sang to it, and laid it down to sleep. People in the village laughed and called it Akua'ba, Akua's child. She did not stop. She carried it to the market, to the river and to the shrine, and she kept hoping.

In time Akua conceived and gave birth to a living child. In one telling the wooden figure had brought the child; in another her patience and her hope had. Other women who had waited long asked for figures of their own, and carvers began to make them, each a small wooden child with a flat, disc-shaped head.

That is how the akua'ba is explained. The story is etiological, a tale told to account for a custom rather than a record of one event. The dolls are still carved and still carried by women hoping to conceive, and girls are given them to practise mothering. Museums now collect them as art, which is a different kind of use from the one the story describes.
notes: The story is etiological: it explains a custom rather than recording a single event, and it is told in several forms. The woman's name, Akua, is also the name of the doll. Museum and ethnographic accounts differ on whether the figure stands for a child, a hoped-for child or a spirit. The dolls are still made and used today, and are also sold as souvenirs.

title: Sasabonsam and the Hunter
source_ref: Akan folktales of the deep forest, recorded in Rattray's collections and in later Ghanaian anthologies
paragraphs: Kwaku was a hunter, and he knew the difference between the farms and the forest beyond them. On the far side of the last field the paths narrow and the trees close over. He went there after duiker, following tracks farther than he meant to, until the light came down in narrow pieces and the birds had stopped. Then he heard nothing at all.

Under the tallest tree in that part of the forest, something was hanging upside down. It was Sasabonsam: long arms, hair like moss, eyes red as embers, teeth that looked like iron. It let itself drop to the path and stood between Kwaku and the way home. Kwaku had fired his one charge at the duiker. He had a knife, which was no use at all.

He did not run. He greeted the creature politely, by the praise-name that hunters use, and laid the duiker on the ground as a gift. Then he said, 'In my village they say no one can hang as you hang. They say you can hold a branch with your feet and let both hands hang free. I have never seen it.' The monster was proud, and it wanted to be seen.

Sasabonsam hooked its feet over a branch and hung there, both arms loose, showing off. Kwaku walked backwards, one slow step at a time, then turned and ran for the boundary of the farms. Behind him the forest screamed, but the creature stopped at the trees. It belongs to the deep forest, not to the fields, and in other versions the hunter escapes by a riddle, a gift or a river.
notes: Sasabonsam is described differently from place to place: a bat-like or ape-like creature hanging in the highest trees, sometimes with iron teeth and blood-red eyes, sometimes a witch's familiar or a warning to children. The trick Kwaku uses here is built from motifs found in several versions, and other tellings end with the hunter killed, rescued, or simply waking at the edge of the farm. No single authoritative text exists.
